prompt.context: Our client is Sally, a retired 'titan of business' now living on Nantucket. She owns a single ice cream shop and has called us to ask whether it is a good idea for her to expand her business into bagels.
prompt.question: Should Sally expand her ice cream shop into bagels? Is it profitable to do so, and if so, how should she produce them?

clarifying_info.q: Does Sally own more than one shop?
clarifying_info.a: No, she owns only one shop.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any motivations besides profitability for expanding into bagels?
clarifying_info.a: No, expanding into bagels is only desired if profitable; there are no other motivations.

clarifying_info.q: What is Nantucket like — is it a year-round destination?
clarifying_info.a: Nantucket is a popular summer vacation destination, so it has very different population sizes in winter versus summer.

framework: Market sizing: estimate total annual bagel market on Nantucket (year-round vs. tourist population segments)
Competition and market share: identify existing bagel suppliers, estimate their market shares, and estimate a realistic share for Sally
Profitability / cost analysis: compare revenue potential against two production options (in-house vs. buying from Joe the baker) and find the indifference point
Risks and implementation: brainstorm factors that could cause sales to fall short of projections

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — How would you calculate the size of the bagel market on Nantucket?
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the market into year-round residents and tourists, noting Nantucket's seasonal nature. Key data: year-round population 10,000; 25% are bagel buyers buying 4 bagels/week. Tourist population adds 30,000 for 6 months; 50% are bagel buyers buying 2 bagels/week. Candidate should compute annual bagel volume for each segment and sum them. Round 52 weeks to 50 when asked.

math.setup: Year-round buyers: 10,000 × 0.25 = 2,500 buyers × 4 bagels/week = 10,000 bagels/week × 50 weeks = 500,000 bagels/year. Tourist buyers: 30,000 × 0.50 = 15,000 buyers × 2 bagels/week = 30,000 bagels/week × 25 weeks ≈ 750,000 bagels/year.
math.answer: Total annual bagel market ≈ 1.25 million bagels

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — What would you estimate the competitor market shares to be, and what share could Sally realistically obtain?
questions.guidance: There are 6 current bagel suppliers: 2 large chains (e.g., Finagle a Bagel), 2 specialty shops, 2 mixed-use stores (health food stores, delis). Candidate should propose a reasonable split acknowledging chains likely dominate. A strong answer: large chains ~50%, specialty shops ~30%, mixed-use ~20%. For Sally's share, a conservative Bain estimate of 10% is appropriate; candidate should justify it.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 — Set up the profitability equations for both production options (in-house vs. buying from Joe) and find the indifference point.
questions.guidance: Revenue: $1.25 per bagel (same price as all competitors). In-house costs: $1,000/month fixed equipment + $0.50/bagel variable. Joe the baker: $0.75/bagel, no fixed cost. Candidate should write both profit equations, set costs equal to find the indifference quantity, then compare to Sally's projected volume of 10,000 bagels/month to recommend the better option.

math.setup: Let x = bagels sold. In-house profit: 1.25x − (1,000 + 0.50x). Buy-from-Joe profit: 1.25x − 0.75x. Indifference when costs are equal: 1,000 + 0.50x = 0.75x.
steps: At Sally's projected 10,000 bagels/month: in-house profit = 0.75(10,000) − 1,000 = $6,500/month; buy-from-Joe profit = 0.50(10,000) = $5,000/month
In-house is more profitable above 4,000 bagels/month; Sally's 10,000/month is more than twice the indifference point
math.answer: Indifference point: 4,000 bagels/month (48,000/year). Since projected volume of 10,000/month exceeds this threshold, Sally should produce in-house.

brainstorming.prompt: Six months later Sally has started producing bagels in-house and selling them, but sales are way below predictions. Why? Generate as many reasons as possible.

categories.name: Product quality
ideas: Inferior bagel product compared to established competitors
Inconsistent quality during early production ramp-up
Production capacity constrained — still learning machines or machines insufficient to reach full volume

categories.name: Marketing and awareness
ideas: Insufficient marketing — customers unaware Sally sells bagels
Poor signage or no advertising to drive trial
No loyalty program or incentives to attract first-time bagel buyers

categories.name: Location and shop setup
ideas: Location of Sally's shop is not convenient for the bagel-buying routine
Shop hours do not match when customers typically buy bagels (e.g., early morning)
No complementary product such as coffee, reducing the basket appeal

categories.name: Competitive response
ideas: Existing competitors responded aggressively — price cuts, promotions, new locations
Competitors opened additional stores near Sally's shop
Customer loyalty to existing bagel shops; buyers unwilling to switch

categories.name: Demand and market conditions
ideas: Overall bagel demand on Nantucket lower than estimated
Seasonal demand mis-timed — expansion launched in off-season
Economy or tourism downturn reducing foot traffic

recommendation: The bagel expansion is financially viable if Sally can achieve the projected 10% market share (~10,000 bagels/month)
At that volume she should produce in-house: it is more profitable than buying from Joe above the 4,000-bagel/month threshold
risks: Actual market share may fall short of 10% given 6 established competitors with loyal customer bases
In-house production carries higher fixed costs ($1,000/month equipment) which create a break-even floor
Seasonal demand swings on Nantucket may make it difficult to maintain volume year-round
next_steps: Conduct a pilot to validate demand before committing to full in-house equipment investment
Develop a marketing plan targeted at both year-round residents and tourists
Evaluate complementary products (coffee, spreads) to improve basket size and foot traffic
